findings.claim: "Sesamoid bones are a fifth category that Edexcel specifically requires"; key fact "Edexcel requires five bone shape categories ... AQA only teaches four categories"; collapsible "The Edexcel mark scheme classifies it as a sesamoid bone".
findings.truth: Spec 1.1.2 names four classifications only: long (leverage), short (weight bearing), flat (protection, broad surface for muscle attachment), irregular (protection and muscle attachment). There is no fifth category and no mark-scheme statement of the kind quoted. The patella is anatomically a sesamoid bone, so the label itself is kept, but it is presented as extra anatomy rather than a required category.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/physical-education-1PE0.md 1.1.2 and 1.1.3

findings.claim: "if you write two conflicting classifications, the mark scheme takes the first answer given, which may be the wrong one"
findings.truth: No such rule exists. Contradictory answers are simply not credited.
findings.evidence: invented procedural claim; no spec or mark-scheme basis

findings.claim: "throwers rely on a long humerus to generate club-head speed"
findings.truth: Club-head speed belongs to golf, not to throwing events. The mechanical point (a long lever raises end-point speed) is correct, so no mark is at risk.
findings.evidence: internal wording slip

findings.claim: "The skeleton performs six functions" (protection, muscle attachment, joints, blood cell production, mineral storage, support).
findings.truth: Spec 1.1.1 names five: protection of vital organs, muscle attachment, joints for movement, platelets and red and white blood cell production, storage of calcium and phosphorus. Support is a real skeletal function taught in every textbook and normally credited, so the extra item is additive rather than wrong.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1.1

findings.claim: "You need to know nine specific movement terms" and "Nine movement terms apply to joints" - eight are then listed.
findings.truth: Eight movements are named in spec 1.1.5: flexion, extension, adduction, abduction, rotation, circumduction, plantar-flexion, dorsi-flexion. The lesson lists exactly those eight.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1.5; internal recount

findings.claim: Q6 mark scheme: "examiner accepts a general point that both are slow-healing connective tissues vs muscles".
findings.truth: A fabricated examiner voice inside a mark scheme. Reworded as a credit instruction.
findings.evidence: brief rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: "do not write 'slow-twitch' or 'fast-twitch' alone as these are informal descriptors"
findings.truth: The spec uses the terms itself - 1.1.10 "Characteristics of fast and slow twitch muscle fibre types" - and the spec glossary defines Type I as "Also known as slow-twitch muscle fibres". The advice would push students away from correct vocabulary.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1.10 and Appendix 5 glossary (Type I / IIa / IIx)

findings.claim: "Sprinters like Dina Asher-Smith have a genetic advantage in Type IIx fibre proportion".
findings.truth: No muscle-biopsy data has been published for this named athlete. The general statement about elite sprinters is sound; the personal attribution is invented.
findings.evidence: no published source for the individual claim

findings.claim: Q1 treats the hamstrings as agonist and quadriceps as antagonist during the downward phase of a squat.
findings.truth: In a squat descent the quadriceps work eccentrically to control knee flexion, so they are the working muscle. This spec never introduces concentric or eccentric contraction, so the simple flexion model is the only one available at this level and the answer is defensible.
findings.evidence: spec has no isotonic/eccentric content (grep returns nothing)

findings.claim: Arteries defined as vessels "that carry oxygenated blood away from the heart" and veins as vessels "that carry deoxygenated blood back to the heart" (in both the dfn data-def and the glossary).
findings.truth: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood - both are named in spec 1.2.2, and 1.2.3 requires students to handle oxygenated and deoxygenated blood correctly. The definitions now key on direction, with the exception stated.
findings.evidence: spec 1.2.2 and 1.2.3

findings.claim: "examiners reward breadth and the ability to link adaptations back to specific sport performance improvements".
findings.truth: A fabricated examiner claim. The advice itself is fine once stated as advice.
findings.evidence: brief rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Key fact: "first class - fulcrum in the middle (FLE/ELF)".
findings.truth: Both strings put the load in the middle. A first-class lever runs load-fulcrum-effort or effort-fulcrum-load, so the ordering is LFE or EFL. The second-class (FLE) and third-class (FEL) strings in the same sentence are correct.
findings.evidence: spec 2.1.1; recomputation of the component order

findings.claim: Second-class lever: "The toes act as the fulcrum ... the body weight (load) acts through the ball of the foot".
findings.truth: The ball of the foot is where the fulcrum sits. Body weight is transmitted down the tibia and acts at the ankle joint, which is why the load sits between the fulcrum (toes) and the effort (calf at the heel).
findings.evidence: spec 2.1.1; standard lever analysis of plantar flexion

findings.claim: Q6 is tariffed "9 marks - Evaluate" on lever systems.
findings.truth: The single nine-mark extended-writing question on this paper is set in Section C on physical training. Movement analysis is examined in Section A, where the top tariff is six marks. Re-tariffed to 6; the band descriptors carry no numeric ranges so they still fit.
findings.evidence: spec assessment overview for this paper (Sections A/B/C) and the assessment information list

findings.claim: "A swimmer performing a tumble turn or a skier leaning into a carved turn also uses sagittal axis rotation."
findings.truth: A tumble turn is a forward somersault: sagittal plane about the frontal axis. The lesson's own Q6 mark scheme says exactly that, so the two contradicted each other. The skier example is kept because a lateral body lean is frontal-plane movement about the sagittal axis.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2.2 and 2.2.3; spec glossary (frontal axis allows flexion and extension)

findings.claim: Q6 is tariffed "9 marks - Evaluate" on planes and axes.
findings.truth: Same as F14 - the nine-mark question is set on physical training, not movement analysis. Re-tariffed to 6.
findings.evidence: spec assessment overview for this paper

findings.claim: "The ten components of fitness are divided into two groups"; skill-related "There are five:" followed by six; conclusion "The five skill-related components are agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed"; description "the ten components".
findings.truth: Spec 3.2.1 names eleven: cardiovascular fitness, strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition, agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time, speed. That is five health-related and six skill-related.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.1; recount of the lesson's own lists

findings.claim: "follow the three-step rule that examiners reward".
findings.truth: A fabricated examiner claim. The three-step advice stands on its own.
findings.evidence: brief rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: "a 16-year-old male who covers 2,400 metres or more scores in the 'excellent' category, while 1,800-2,000 metres is 'below average'".
findings.truth: Published Cooper 12-minute run norms for males aged 15-16 are: excellent above 2,800 m; above average 2,500-2,800 m; average 2,300-2,499 m; below average 2,200-2,299 m; poor below 2,200 m. The lesson's figures also contradicted Lesson 17, which quotes 2,800 m for excellent.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Cooper test normative table (males 15-16)

findings.claim: SMART targets taught with "Mark schemes credit only targets that satisfy all five criteria simultaneously" and "For Explain questions on SMART targets, examiners expect all five criteria to be referenced".
findings.truth: SMART targets are spec 2.2.2, in the sport psychology topic of the second written paper, and are assessed in the personal exercise programme. They are not in the physical training content of this paper. The explanation of SMART is kept because it is used in the programme; the two exam claims are corrected.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2.2 (second written paper) and the personal exercise programme criteria

findings.claim: "mark schemes award half marks for one-sided answers".
findings.truth: Half marks are not awarded on this qualification. A one-sided answer simply cannot reach full marks.
findings.evidence: invented mark-scheme rule

findings.claim: Q4 is tariffed at 3 marks but its mark scheme lists only two mark points.
findings.truth: A third creditable point exists: the load and repetition scheme decides which adaptation occurs, so the same exercise trains either component. Added so the scheme matches the tariff.
findings.evidence: internal recount of the mark scheme

findings.claim: Key fact groups the banned substances as "anabolic steroids, EPO and blood doping, growth hormones, stimulants, narcotic analgesics, diuretics, beta blockers".
findings.truth: Spec 3.5.5 groups them as anabolic steroids, beta blockers, diuretics, narcotic analgesics, peptide hormones (EPO and growth hormone), stimulants, blood doping. EPO and growth hormone belong together as peptide hormones, and blood doping is a separate category, not a partner to EPO. The conclusion in the same lesson lists eight items, so the two disagreed.
findings.evidence: spec 3.5.5

findings.claim: Cooper normative bands given as excellent above 2,800 m, above average 2,400-2,800 m, average 2,000-2,400 m, below average 1,600-2,000 m, poor below 1,600 m.
findings.truth: Published norms for males 15-16: above average 2,500-2,800 m, average 2,300-2,499 m, below average 2,200-2,299 m, poor below 2,200 m. The excellent threshold was already right, and the worked example (2,550 m = above average) still holds after the correction.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Cooper test normative table (males 15-16)

findings.claim: Q5 mark scheme: "Ben's absolute improvement (6 press-ups) is the same as Marcus's but Ben's relative improvement is 42.9% due to a lower starting point".
findings.truth: Marcus went 18 to 26, an improvement of 8, not 6. Ben went 14 to 20, an improvement of 6. The reasoning is also inverted: Ben starts lower (14 against 18) yet has the smaller relative gain (42.9% against 44.4%). Every percentage in the scheme recomputes correctly (31.8, 44.4, 16.7, 42.9) and Marcus is correctly named the greatest improver.
findings.evidence: recomputation from the question's own table

findings.claim: Invented procedural mark-scheme claims recur across the unit: "the mark scheme expects three elements ... Missing any one of these costs marks" (L8), "the mark scheme requires justified reasoning" (L7), "Mark schemes reward the link" (L12), "the mark scheme requires them" (L5), "Examiners will not award marks for" (L17), "typically score half marks" (L8).
findings.truth: All are unsourced. Each is generic and sound exam advice once the mark-scheme attribution is stripped, so only the concrete false ones (F2, F6, F11, F18, F20, F21) are edited. Worth a fleet-wide sweep of this phrasing rather than lesson-by-lesson edits.
findings.evidence: pattern across L5, L7, L8, L12, L17

findings.claim: "A midfielder covers around 10 km per match ... with approximately 50-100 maximal sprints."
findings.truth: Distance is right. Published match-analysis figures put outfield sprints nearer 20-40 per match depending on the sprint definition, so 50-100 is high. The point being made (mixed energy systems) is unaffected.
findings.evidence: match-analysis literature; no exam claim rests on the figure

findings.claim: Q1 (multiple choice) and knowledge check 1 both require "sesamoid" as the classification of the patella, while the spec offers only long, short, flat and irregular.
findings.truth: Two options. (a) Leave both as they are: sesamoid is anatomically correct, is what PE textbooks teach, and the corrected prose now says it is extra anatomy - my recommendation, because the alternative forces a wrong answer. (b) Replace the patella item with a bone whose classification is unambiguous under the four spec categories (for example, classify the scapula or a vertebra). Option (b) is safer against the spec letter but loses a genuinely useful misconception.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1.2 (four categories) against 1.1.3 (patella named as a bone to know)
findings.ruling: NOTE: sesamoid kept as an MCQ/KC answer - anatomically right, prose now frames it as beyond the four spec categories.

findings.claim: Every extended-response mark scheme in the unit uses the band names Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging.
findings.truth: These are not on the validator's banned list, so nothing blocks them, but they are not the house vocabulary either (Top band / Upper-mid band / Mid band / Lower-mid band / Low band). Recommendation: leave them for this unit and decide once, fleet-wide, rather than rewriting 17 lessons here.
findings.evidence: house band vocabulary in the checker brief
findings.ruling: NOTE: band names left for the programme-wide band-ladder sweep.

summary: 17 lessons checked against the spec. Four mark-affecting errors: a first-class lever written as FLE/ELF (load in the middle), a swimming tumble turn taught as sagittal-axis rotation, ten components of fitness where the spec names eleven, and a press-up data mark scheme that misstates one athlete's improvement. Sesamoid bone is taught as a required fifth classification the spec does not have. Every calculation in the unit was recomputed: cardiac output, training zones, minute ventilation and all percentage-change answers are correct, but two Cooper normative tables were wrong and contradicted each other. Six fabricated examiner or mark-scheme claims fixed, and two nine-mark questions on movement analysis re-tariffed to six because the extended question is set on physical training.
